 `channels.ts` and `pairing.ts` in `src/remote/` are the serve side; `channels-client.ts` is the shell side and `src/tui/channels-surface.ts` the modal, sidebar row and readline text, all drawn from one snapshot. `serve` always mints the shell token on a loopback listener and answers seven `/v1/remote/channels-*` routes (`status`, `pair`, `pairing`, `cancel`, `reload`, `test`, `disconnect`), even with no config. The bot token never travels over HTTP: the shell writes `remote/bot-token` and `remote/config.json` itself (atomic, mode 600), then asks `serve` to reload without a restart. Pairing runs inside the single poller: a one-time code (10 minutes, single use) in a private message adds the sender to the allowlist, and the `my_chat_member` event of the bot being added to a group gives the group id, after which `serve` checks that it is a forum and the bot may manage topics. Test posts to General naming the host; Disconnect has `serve` delete every topic and stop, then the shell erases the files, or erases them alone and reports that topics remain when `serve` is down. One bot per machine.
 
 ## Explicitly out of scope
 
 - The serve `/v1/approvals` surface: an approval raised there has no Telegram card. The Allow/Deny buttons here belong to a mirrored shell session and travel over the shell-token routes.
 - Telegram verification beyond the fake Bot API (topic creation, permissions, callbacks, the 409 case).

the orchestrator holds.
 - It must answer JSON, `{"order": [...]}`, best first, and must place the session's
   own model. An id that was not discovered is dropped. An agent error, a
   timeout, a malformed answer, or one that leaves out the session's model
   resolves to the session's model, exactly as without an agent.
 - It never places `standard` or `deep` below the session: `deep` is only ever taken
   from above the session in its order, `standard` is never asked. A larger
   class of an older generation that costs more than the session's model is
   refused whatever it says.
 - The result is cached by a hash of the candidate catalogue with prices, so an
   identical catalogue asks once.
 - It runs on the **light** tier of the session's own provider — the cheap step
   below the session, or the session model itself when nothing sits below.
 - A resolution it produced is recorded `tier_resolution: agent-ranked`.
 
 ## Where this actually runs
 
 Two places, and they are not the same shape:
 
 - **`spawn_subagent`** (`src/harness/tool/builtin/spawn-subagent-tool.ts`) takes an
-  optional `model_tier` input and does the rest in code: it builds the tier map
-  with `buildTierMap` from its host's detection result, hands it to
-  `resolveChildModel`, and records the outcome on the dispatch's run trace.
-  Omitting `model_tier` inherits the parent's model, exactly as before the field
-  existed.
+  optional `model_class` input (`light`, `standard`, `expert`, `frontier`) and lets
+  model routing choose the child's model from it. It still accepts `model_tier` but
+  ignores it and logs a migration notice (`SPAWN_SUBAGENT_IGNORED_FIELDS`). Omitting
+  `model_class` leaves the child to the project's subagent routing: the parent's
+  model unless that category is set to `auto`.
 - **An orchestrator authoring a dispatch document** *runs a command*:
   `keryx review tier`. It takes the signals below as flags and prints the `model`
   block ready to paste — the tier, the ordered rule ids that produced it, the
   resolved provider/model, `tier_resolution` and `model_discovery`. `--json`
   prints the block alone.
 
 An orchestrator is an agent following prose and **cannot call a TypeScript
 function**: asked for a tier by hand it reads a table of signals and does the
 arithmetic in its head — the exact mechanical work this programme moves out of
 skills and into the code that consumes them. `keryx review tier` is that code's
 entry point; `decideDispatchModel` is what it calls.
 
 Nothing reads a recorded resolution back and checks it. These fields explain a
 finished run; they do not gate one.
 
 ## A third place: compiling a Claude Code subagent file
 
 `keryx agents export --runtime claude` (`src/agents/compile.ts`'s
 `renderClaudeExport`) is neither of the two shapes above — it never asks
 `spawn_subagent` or `keryx review tier` anything, and it runs at EXPORT time,

```bash
 keryx review blast-radius --ref "${BASE_SHA}" --previous blast-radius.json [--final]
 ```
 
 It prints the decision and the reason, and reuses the previous record when
 nothing moved. The final round recomputes whatever the file set did — otherwise a
 fix introduced in round 3 gets no regression check at all, and the round that
 certifies the flow is the one that checked the least.
 
 ## Readiness — the checklist behind `completed` and behind publishing
 
 `keryx review readiness <review-id-or-path> [--json]` reads the package and prints every readiness item, READY or NOT READY, each with the evidence and the command that repairs it. It writes nothing, and exits non-zero when the verdict is NOT READY. Only item 9 reaches GitHub (the PR's own file list); the TUI and `review status` read the package alone.
 
 1. `files-covered` — every changed file is in a wave or carries a recorded waiver.
 2. `blast-radius` — no file the blast radius cut is left unreviewed. A cut radius writes `chunks.json`; run `keryx review chunks plan`, `estimate`, `next`/`record`, `merge`. Then bring in what the passes found: `merge` lists the findings and how many `findings.json` lacks; `keryx review ingest --review-id <id>` records them as `review-regression/<chunk>`; ingest and the report are repeated when a pass finished after the report was written. `review complete` warns about a pass finding still out of `findings.json` and does not refuse. In an unattended run every wave runs without a question, up to the 25-pass ceiling; in an interactive run the operator is asked once: in keryx shell call `review_chunks_answer` (a card, never a terminal); elsewhere the operator runs `keryx review chunks estimate --package <dir> --answer yes --quote "<their words>"` in their terminal; unattended, record Not run.
 3. `reviewers` — every planned reviewer was dispatched and its result ingested.
 4. `verifier` — the verifier checked every blocker/major finding, or the operator waived the item; a `Not verified: N` line in the report no longer passes it.
 5. `ledger` — the ledger is READY.
 6. `coverage-md` — coverage.md does not list a reviewer as `run` that the dispatch record says did not finish. Re-run `keryx review ingest` for the package.
-7. `head` — the report's head is the PR head.
+7. `head` — the head recorded at `review start` is still the PR head and the PR is not merged; otherwise only the operator's `head` waiver lifts it (no report line does).
 8. `report-names` — pending mutation candidates and parity warnings are named in the report.
 9. `pr-files` — the changed-file count equals the PR's own file list. A recount more than 3x the recorded scope is refused: it came from the wrong base. Recount with `keryx review blast-radius --package <ref> --changed <the PR's files>`.

 11. `premise-decisions` — every finding `review-premise` held (`challenged` or `owner-decision`) has an operator decision: in keryx shell the card `review_decide_premise`; elsewhere ask the operator with the host's question tool and record the answer with `keryx review decide-premise --package <dir> --finding <global_id> --answer uphold|dismiss --reason "<why>" --answered-by <source>:<ref> --answer-text "<their words>" --question-text "<the question>"` (SKILL.md "Wave D"; the record reads `confirmedVia: "host-question"`).
